clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute appendicitis until proven otherwise evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute appendicitis until proven otherwise is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, securing IV access and fluids, providing analgesia, obtaining urgent bloods and imaging, and referring urgently to surgery for likely appendicectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: acute right-sided abdominal pain for 12 hours

Key HPI features: pain started around the umbilicus last night then migrated to the right lower quadrant, now 8/10 and constant, sharper with movement or coughing, walking hunched over eases it slightly, vomited twice this morning, subjective fever (checked at home, 38.2°C), no bowel motion or flatus since the pain started
Objective/Exam findings: Vitals, abdominal exam (McBurney's point, Rovsing's, psoas/obturator signs), FBC, CRP, urinalysis, imaging (ultrasound or CT) as indicated.
Relevant background/PMH: no previous episodes like this, no previous abdominal surgery
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute appendicitis until proven otherwise.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: diffuse rigidity or rebound tenderness beyond McBurney's point, high fever with marked tachycardia, signs of sepsis (hypotension, marked tachycardia, or altered mental status).
management_principles: NPO, IV access and fluids, analgesia, urgent bloods and imaging, surgical referral for likely appendicectomy
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Elicit the classic migratory pattern of appendicitis pain using OPQRST
Screen for peritonism red flags (fever, guarding, anorexia, vomiting)
Address the patient's ICE — specifically his fear of rupture
Verbalise the surgical abdomen differential and next steps clearly

teaching.one_liner: Obstruction and inflammation of the appendix causes pain that classically migrates from around the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant, worsened by movement or coughing, with vomiting and fever — a surgical emergency treated as appendicitis until proven otherwise.
red_flags: Diffuse rigidity or rebound tenderness beyond McBurney's point — suggests perforation and peritonitis
High fever with marked tachycardia — suggests progression to perforation or abscess
Signs of sepsis (hypotension, marked tachycardia, altered mental status)

must_ask.say: Did the pain start somewhere else, like around your belly button, before moving to the right side?
Have you had any nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite along with the pain?
Does the pain get worse with movement, coughing, or going over bumps in the car?
Have you had any fever or chills since the pain started?
Have you had any changes in your bowel movements, or any burning when you urinate?

differentials: Urinary tract infection or renal colic

exam.finding: Patient appears in acute distress, lying still on the examination couch with knees slightly flexed, grimacing with movement.
Blood pressure 126/82 mmHg, heart rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 38.2°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Abdomen is flat with no surgical scars, rashes, distension, or visible peristalsis.
Hypoactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants; no bruits heard.
Normal tympany heard throughout; no dullness over the flanks.
Soft with focal tenderness and involuntary guarding in the right lower quadrant; other quadrants are soft and non-tender.
Localized rebound tenderness present in the right lower quadrant, with no generalized peritonitis.
Negative Murphy's sign; no tenderness or inspiratory arrest on palpation of the right upper quadrant.
Positive McBurney's point tenderness, positive Rovsing's sign with pain referred to the right lower quadrant, and positive psoas sign on the right.
No masses felt; focal tenderness on the right side of the rectal vault; no blood on the glove.
